criterion_notes.c1: The paper focuses topically on rural community drinking water services (Rural Potable Water / APR systems managed by community water organizations) in Chile, discussing sustainability, coverage, intermittent supply, water quality, and tariff recovery.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: YES — the paper examines legal, regulatory, institutional, and governance factors in Chilean rural drinking water services, including community water organization (CWO) oversight, water rights, tariff setting, private technical service providers, and Law No. 20.998 (2017). Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: UNCLEAR (doctrinally yes, empirically no) — Law No. 20.998 establishes concrete rule-type mechanisms governing rural water provision (5-year CWO licensing requirements conditioned on water rights and reserve funds, mandatory tariff cost-recovery structures, restrictions on municipal operation, public registration/bidding for private contractors, and enforcement fines under Article 89), but the empirical Delphi survey was conducted in 2016 prior to the 2017 passage of Law No. 20.998 and only asked experts to rate 34 broad sustainability drivers rather than empirically testing how a specific rule-type mechanism governs service access. Under both readings of Criterion 2, the study is excluded due to lack of an empirical access outcome (E04).
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary empirical data from a structured 4-round Delphi survey of 14 Chilean rural water sector experts (selected from 23 qualified candidates) conducted in 2016 using quantitative consensus metrics (sum, median, absolute deviation, IQR, range) and qualitative panelist comments, paired with a non-empirical prospective policy analysis of Law No. 20.998 (2017).
criterion_notes.c4: NO — the primary empirical component measures only 14 experts' Likert-scale importance ratings (1 to 5) and consensus/non-consensus rankings of 34 perceived drivers of rural water system sustainability. It does not measure or report primary empirical outcomes on household or community water access, connection, service availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion (all rural coverage, outage, and cost-recovery figures cited in the text are secondary background statistics from prior reports).
criterion_notes.c5: NO — while the 4-round Delphi study design and 14-expert panel are identifiable, the study does not link an identifiable governance/rule-type exposure to an empirical household, community, or utility service-access outcome; Law No. 20.998 was passed in 2017 after the 2016 Delphi data collection and had not yet been implemented or empirically evaluated.

evidence_quotes.quote: We draw our insights from a Delphi analysis conducted in 2016, prior to the passage of the new law asking Chilean rural water sector experts to identify factors that influence the sustainability of rural water service delivery in Chile.

The new regulation aims to strengthen the management capacity of community organizations, address deficits in tariffs through implementing a tariff structure covering service operation, establish stronger rights and obligations for CWOs and operators, and strengthen the ability of the central government to enforce norms.

In order to acquire a licence, CWOs must demonstrate the possession of water rights, sufficient service quality, the availability of reserve funds, the existence of an investment plan, pricing schedules, and financial statements, which must be approved by the SAPR (Donoso, 2018).

We elicited expert opinion on drivers and their importance in four survey rounds. Round 1 required expert to list and define the drivers that influence the sustainability of rural water services in Chile.

Further research to trace the implementation of Law No. 20.998 and identify the conditions under which CWOs are more likely to be in line with the new law will help to provide insights for countries that, like Chile, want to address the inequities of quality and challenges of sustainability in rural water services.

raw_response.exposure: No empirical legal or governance exposure tested on water users or service systems; panelists rated 34 candidate sustainability drivers (including regulatory/legal framework, CWO management, adequate tariffs, and water rights), which the authors prospectively compare against Chile's Law No. 20.998 (enacted in 2017, after the 2016 Delphi survey)
raw_response.outcome: Expert Likert-scale importance ratings (1 to 5) and non-parametric consensus rankings across 34 perceived drivers of rural water service sustainability (no primary household, community, or system-level service access outcome measured)
raw_response.population_and_sample: 14 Chilean rural water sector experts (out of 23 invited: 4 academics, 1 lawyer in rural water rights, 2 private water service consultants, 1 water committee member, and 5 government officials); unit of analysis is the expert panelist
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E04 (Wrong outcome). Although the paper addresses rural drinking water governance in Chile and discusses rule-type provisions of Law No. 20.998 (2017) — such as 5-year CWO licensing requirements, tariff cost-recovery structures, restrictions on municipal operation, registration/bidding of private consultancies, and regulatory sanctions — its sole empirical component is a 2016 4-round Delphi survey of 14 sector experts carried out before Law No. 20.998 was enacted. The empirical outcome reported is expert consensus and Likert-scale importance rankings of 34 general drivers perceived to affect rural water sustainability, with no primary empirical measurement of household or community water access, connection, availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion (and all sector coverage/outage statistics are cited solely as secondary background). Thus, the paper is excluded under both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and the plain wording of Criterion 2.
raw_response.study_design: Four-round Delphi expert panel survey (n = 14) conducted in 2016 combined with prospective policy analysis of Law No. 20.998 (2017)
